issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette: Mark, a 21-year-old European man, works in social ministry and was married just last year. His life took a dramatic turn when he served as a relief worker in a war zone. The traumatic event that has left lasting marks on his psyche occurred during one of the missions where an explosion rocked the area while he was trying to distribute aid. The memory of that day remains vivid, and it is hard for Mark to believe that such extreme violence actually happened to him. Since returning home, any mention of military topics or hearing shouting in Arabic triggers intense reactions within him. These triggers often lead to nightmares and flashbacks, compelling him to ruminate on how the event could have been prevented if only he had acted differently. This constant rumination is one of his maladaptive strategies, along with staying up very late to avoid falling asleep for fear that he won't wake up from another nightmarish dream. Mark's wife has noticed a significant change in him since he returned. He avoids situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful because the contrast between those moments and his traumatic experiences feels too stark. His memory of the event is so intense that it feels like it’s happening right now rather than something from the past, which makes him relive the terror repeatedly. The memories are exacerbated by his triggers, making it impossible for Mark to function normally at times. For instance, when he hears shouting in Arabic or discusses military topics, he often wakes up during the night to check whether he is safe, driven by a deep-seated belief that strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations pose a threat. This sense of threat from others and his waking alertness only serves to reinforce his memory. He feels as if the danger is always looming, and this heightened state of vigilance makes it difficult for Mark to distinguish between real threats and perceived ones. His fear becomes self-reinforcing; each trigger leads him back into a cycle of rumination and hyper-vigilance. As Mark’s occupation involves interacting with people in various communities, his condition has affected how he performs his duties. He avoids going to certain areas or events where he might encounter triggers that could set off the cycle again. This avoidance behavior has strained his relationships at work, leading him to miss important meetings and community gatherings. What frightens Mark most is the thought of never being able to return to a state of normalcy without these intrusive memories and heightened fears. His maladaptive strategies, like delaying sleep and ruminating about how he could have prevented the event, have only exacerbated his symptoms over time. The cycle feels unbreakable, as each element reinforces the other. Mark finally sought help after realizing that he couldn't manage his condition on his own. He is hoping for relief from the constant fear and terror that plague him daily. His biggest hope is to regain control of his life without the overwhelming sense of threat and the relentless reminders of the event that continue to haunt him.
